editorial.headline: The Craft of Skills: Private Creative-Industry Training
editorial.standfirst: A private vocational-training activity spanning craft, fashion, leatherwork and beauty skills—with full national foreign-ownership openness and no Bali moratorium block.
editorial.body:
KBLI 85573 covers private vocational training for the creative industries. Its subject matter is practical: training designed to add skills or expertise in metal and wood carving; crochet, embroidery and weaving; screen printing and plaiting; hand-drawn and stamped batik; leather tanning and finishing; leather-product making; sewing for knitting and woven work; pattern techniques; fashion design and fashion technology; and skin and hair beauty. It is a broad craft-to-fashion remit, but its defining purpose is clear: building occupational capability through training conducted by private providers.

The record makes this activity available across every listed business scale: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth matters because the activity can accommodate highly specialised instruction as well as a wider training operation, while remaining anchored in the same practical aim of adding skills and expertise in creative-industry fields. The scope is not framed around one medium or one trade; it brings together manual techniques, apparel knowledge, leatherwork and beauty instruction under a single private training activity.

Nationally, the PMA status is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the record permits foreign ownership up to that full ceiling for this activity at the national level. The cited PMA basis is Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. There is no need to soften that position with assumptions drawn from adjacent activities or from the diversity of the curriculum: the national entry in this record is expressly open.

Bali must be read on its own terms. The provincial moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities, island-wide and permanently. This activity is not blocked by that moratorium. The record identifies its OSS risk at the Large scale as Medium-High/High, which is why it sits outside the stated moratorium block. For a foreign investor, Bali therefore does not bar PMA registration for this activity under the moratorium described here; its Bali status is recorded as OK or higher risk, rather than as a prohibition.
